questions.q: In this design, what does a Stream actually do?
options: It only tracks which rows changed since it was last read — it never writes or changes data itself
It writes a MERGE statement automatically
It permanently deletes old rows from the source table
It sends an email to Finance when a refund is issued
questions.explain: A Stream is a read-only change tracker. The MERGE that actually writes data is always run by a Task, never by the Stream itself.

questions.q: Why does this design use one shared pair of tables instead of two separate, independently-loaded pipelines for Support and Finance?
options: Two independently-loaded copies of the same data can silently drift apart with no easy way to tell until someone compares totals by hand
Snowflake only allows one pipeline per database
Separate pipelines would cost more in storage than Snowflake allows
There's no real reason — one shared pipeline is just a style preference
questions.explain: A shared foundation means there's only one place the data can be wrong, instead of two pipelines that can each develop their own inconsistency.

questions.q: Why is ticket_facts a current-state table, but refund_events is append-only?
options: A ticket has one current status at a time, but a ticket could have more than one distinct refund event over time
Append-only tables are simply faster in every case
Current-state tables can't hold numeric columns
There's no real difference between the two designs
questions.explain: Support cares about a ticket's latest state (current-state table); Finance cares about every refund that happened (a log of events, not a snapshot).

questions.q: What is the raw JSON landing table named in this chapter's design?
options: raw.tickets_api_raw
marts.ticket_facts
marts.refund_events
staging.tickets_clean
questions.explain: raw.tickets_api_raw holds the untouched ticketing API payload in a VARIANT column, before anything is parsed.

questions.q: Why does this lesson say the distinction between current-state and append-only tables matters later in this chapter, not just now?
options: Because the real bug in Lessons 13-15 happens specifically because one of the two tables tolerates duplicate writes with no visible harm, and one does not
Because Power BI requires knowing this distinction to connect at all
Because Snowflake deletes current-state tables automatically after 30 days
It doesn't actually matter later — this is just a naming convention
questions.explain: An idempotent UPDATE-based MERGE tolerates being run twice; an append-only INSERT-only MERGE does not — that gap is exactly where the chapter's bug lives.
